title: Computational entanglement distillation beyond pure states: efficient protocols and fundamental limitations
authors: Takeru Utsumi, Jacopo Rizzo, Ryuji Takagi, Lorenzo Leone
abstract: The information-theoretic approach to entanglement typically relies on arbitrarily many input copies and unboundedly complex operations; however, the available resources are constrained in reality. This motivates the study of entanglement theory with limited resources. One of its central questions is which quantities characterize entanglement manipulations, and so far, only the idealized case of pure states has been well explored. In this work, we address entanglement distillation from mixed states and identify the Rényi coherent information as the quantity determining the optimal rate in the worst case under two distinct resource constraints. We first characterize the sample-efficient regime, in which unbounded computational power is allowed. Our universal protocol achieves this rate without knowledge of the input state under certain polynomial rank constraints. This rate is optimal among universal protocols: we construct states whose distillable entanglement is nearly extensive, yet from which no universal sample-efficient protocol attains a rate above their Rényi coherent information. We then push this characterization to the computationally efficient frontier: the same bound holds for any efficient protocol even when the input state is known, and another universal protocol achieves this rate efficiently under additional polynomial constraints on the marginal ranks. Overall, our results give the Rényi coherent information a novel operational meaning in two computational settings: universal distillation with limited copies and efficient distillation even with knowledge of the input state.
summary: This work advances the theory of entanglement distillation by moving beyond idealized pure-state assumptions to mixed states under resource constraints. It rigorously proves that the Rényi coherent information dictates the optimal distillation rate for both limited-copy and computationally efficient protocols. This provides a novel operational meaning for this information-theoretic quantity in practical quantum information tasks.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of characterizing entanglement distillation rates from mixed quantum states when physical resources, such as the number of available copies or computational power, are limited.
main_result: The Rényi coherent information is identified as the optimal rate-determining quantity for entanglement distillation in both the sample-efficient (limited copies) and computationally efficient regimes.
method: The authors develop and analyze universal one-way LOCC protocols for distillation, employing information-theoretic bounds derived from Rényi entropy and comparing them against achievable rates under specific resource constraints.
model_or_system: The study focuses on bipartite quantum states (mixed states) shared between two parties (Alice and Bob) on $\Theta(n)$ qubits, aiming to distill ebits using local operations and classical communication (LOCC).
key_observables: Rényi coherent information ($eI_ eta$), information-theoretic distillable entanglement ($ED$), and the distillation rate ($R$).
important_parameters: The analysis hinges on the resource constraints: limited copies ($k=	ext{poly}(n)$) and polynomial circuit size, as well as the state rank.
main_assumptions: The results rely on constructing specific families of mixed states (e.g., 'spike states') and assuming polynomial rank constraints for the most efficient protocols.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the idealized information-theoretic bounds, then tackling the sample-efficient regime, followed by the computationally efficient frontier, culminating in the characterization of the rate by the Rényi coherent information in both constrained settings.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous, resource-aware framework for quantifying entanglement, which is crucial for designing realistic quantum communication protocols that must operate under physical limitations.
